subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Seatbelt's 85 Percent Drop
description: A 60-second lesson on The Seatbelt's 85 Percent Drop.

hook.text: Before seatbelts were common, being thrown from a car in a crash was almost always fatal.

buildup.text: Ejected passengers hit pavement, trees, or other cars at the speed they were traveling.

discovery.text: Wearing a belt reduces fatal injury risk by about 45 percent for front-seat passengers.

twist.text: For ejection deaths specifically, seatbelts cut the risk by roughly 85 percent.

climax.text: Yet even today, about half of all crash fatalities involve people who weren't wearing a belt.

punchline.text: The simplest safety device is still the most ignored.

quiz.question: By roughly how much do seatbelts reduce ejection deaths?

details.summary: Studies consistently show that wearing a seatbelt reduces the risk of fatal injury by roughly 45 percent in cars and up to 85 percent in pickup trucks and SUVs prone to rollover ejection.
details.whyItMatters: Despite being the simplest and cheapest safety device, seatbelts remain the most effective. The staggering reduction in fatality risk demonstrates why universal belt use remains a critical public health goal.
takeaways: Seatbelts cut fatality risk by about 45 percent in passenger cars
In rollovers the risk reduction can reach 85 percent by preventing ejection
Thousands of lives could be saved yearly with full compliance

faq.question: Why is the fatality reduction higher in rollovers than frontal crashes?
faq.answer: In rollovers, unbelted occupants are thrown around the cabin or ejected through windows, which is almost always fatal. Seatbelts keep occupants inside the protective cabin, eliminating the ejection risk.

faq.question: What percentage of car occupants still do not wear seatbelts?
faq.answer: In the United States about 8 to 10 percent of front-seat occupants do not wear seatbelts. Rear-seat usage is lower. Unbelted occupants are vastly overrepresented in traffic fatality statistics.
